# On the Peculiar Comfort of Small Routines

I've been thinking lately about the unremarkable moments that somehow hold our lives together. Not the big ones—not birthdays or achievements or disasters. I mean the tiny, almost invisible routines that we perform without thinking, the small rituals that might seem pointless until you realize that their pointlessness is precisely what makes them valuable.

There's something about making coffee the same way every morning that feels like an anchor. Not because coffee itself is meaningful, but because the repetition creates a kind of baseline for existence. The specific sequence of movements—the filter, the water temperature, the wait—becomes almost meditative. It's not meditation in the intentional sense, where you're trying to achieve some higher state. It's more like your hands know what to do while your mind gets to wander. And that wandering, I think, is where most of my actual thinking happens.

I wonder if this is what people mean when they talk about "presence" or "mindfulness," though those words have become so laden with wellness culture that they've almost lost meaning. What I'm talking about is simpler: the way your attention can relax into a familiar motion, the way you stop struggling against routine and instead let it carry you. There's a freedom in that, somehow.

This probably sounds like I'm trying to make something profound out of nothing, which is maybe fair. But I think there's a reason people cling to routines, especially during difficult periods. It's not because the routine fixes anything. It's because it provides proof that some things can still work as expected, that causality hasn't completely broken down, that if you put the coffee grounds in the filter, water will eventually become coffee. In a chaotic world, that's not nothing.

I've also been noticing how much of life is just adjacent to the things we actually care about. Like, the moment you have with a friend isn't really the dinner—it's the half hour before when you're both kind of distracted, getting ready, maybe putting on music you haven't heard in years and unexpectedly feeling emotional about it. The actual dinner might be nice, but it's surrounded by this ambient quality of something mattering, and that's often more important than the main event itself.

This is why I think we're suspicious of optimization, even when we claim to want it. We say we want "efficient" meetings or "streamlined" processes, but what we've actually learned, often painfully, is that the good parts of life happen in the margins. The joke made while waiting for the meeting to start. The tangent that goes nowhere but somehow makes you trust the other person more. The inefficiency is where the texture is.

I read something recently about how modern life has stripped away a lot of the forced waiting that used to be built into existence. You used to have to wait for trains, wait for letters, wait for things to happen. That waiting wasn't pleasant necessarily, but it created these pockets of time that were genuinely yours, time you couldn't fill with obligation. Now we're trying to fill every moment with productivity or entertainment, and I think we're paying a price for it that we're not entirely acknowledging.

There's also something interesting about how we relate to things that serve no purpose. Like, why do people keep plants they don't care about? Why do we make our beds when we're just going to get back in them? Why do some people arrange their books by color or keep shells from beaches they visited decades ago? These are acts of creating meaning in a world that doesn't require them. They're almost defiant. They're saying: I get to decide what matters, even if it matters to no one else.

I think about this especially when I notice someone has organized their bookshelf or decorated their apartment in a way that clearly took thought and effort and won't impress most visitors. There's something beautiful about that—about doing things that are good because you decided they're good, not because they're effective or impressive. It's a kind of freedom that's harder to come by than we usually admit.

The difficulty, of course, is that our entire economic and social structure is built on the premise that things should be optimized, that time should be valuable, that efficiency is always good. There's a constant pressure to be "productive," to turn hobbies into side hustles, to monetize your interests, to ensure that even your leisure time is generating some kind of return. It's exhausting just thinking about it.

And yet, people keep doing things that serve no purpose, and I think that's genuinely important. We keep small traditions alive. We write letters by hand sometimes even though email is faster. We take the long way home for no reason. We remember details about people that have nothing to do with how useful they are. We're constantly, quietly insisting that life is more than its productive output, even if we don't always say it out loud.

I suppose what I'm trying to say, if I'm trying to say anything, is that I've found myself grateful for impractical things lately. For rituals that don't lead anywhere. For the kind of boredom that lets your mind settle. For people who take time with you even when time is money. For routines that have no purpose except that you've decided they have one.

The world is loud and fast and always asking what you're going to do next, what the point is, whether this is efficient. It's nice to step out of that sometimes. It's nice to just make coffee the same way you always do, or watch the light change in a room you know well, or think about nothing in particular while your hands do something they've learned to do without you.

Maybe that's all this was. Just me thinking out loud about how the small, pointless things have become important to me. How the routines I used to dismiss as mundane now feel like secret acts of resistance. How I've learned to appreciate being alive in the margins, in the moments between the important things, which turn out to be where most of life actually happens.

That's worth writing about, I think. Even if it doesn't go anywhere.
